prompt: When my MQTT 5.0 client encodes a PUBREL, which packet type number goes in the top nibble of byte 1 and what do the lower four flag bits have to be?

forbidden.note: PUBREL reserved bits are 0010, not all zero.

provenance: Packet type and reserved flag values come from section 3.6.1 (PUBREL Fixed Header) and Table 2-2 in section 2.1.3.
reference_answer: PUBREL is MQTT Control Packet type 6. Its reserved flag bits 3-0 must be 0,0,1,0 (nibble 0010), giving a first byte of 0x62. Any other flag value is treated as malformed and the Network Connection is closed [MQTT-3.6.1-1]. See section 3.6.1 and Table 2-2 in section 2.1.3.

prompt: My broker drops SUBSCRIBE packets my client builds with a first byte of 0x80. Under MQTT 5.0, what packet type and flag nibble should SUBSCRIBE carry, and which way does it flow?
provenance: Type number and reserved bits come from section 3.8.1 and Table 2-2 in 2.1.3; the direction from section 3.8.
reference_answer: SUBSCRIBE is packet type 8 and is only sent from Client to Server (section 3.8, Table 2-1 in 2.1.2). Bits 3-0 of byte 1 are reserved and must be 0,0,1,0, so the first byte is 0x82. A Server treats any other flag value as malformed and closes the Network Connection [MQTT-3.8.1-1] (section 3.8.1, Table 2-2 in 2.1.3).

prompt: For an MQTT 5.0 UNSUBSCRIBE, what control packet type value do I put in byte 1 and which reserved flag pattern is required?
provenance: Values come from section 3.10.1 (UNSUBSCRIBE Fixed Header) and Table 2-2 in section 2.1.3.
reference_answer: UNSUBSCRIBE is MQTT Control Packet type 10, sent Client to Server. Its reserved bits 3-0 must be 0,0,1,0, so byte 1 is 0xA2. The Server must treat any other value as malformed and close the Network Connection [MQTT-3.10.1-1]. See section 3.10.1 and Table 2-2 in section 2.1.3.

prompt: In MQTT 5.0, what is CONNACK's packet type value, who sends it, and can a broker send it more than once on the same connection?
provenance: Type value from section 3.2.1 and Table 2-1 in section 2.1.2; the single-CONNACK rule from section 3.2.
reference_answer: CONNACK is MQTT Control Packet type 2 with all four flag bits reserved as 0 (first byte 0x20). It flows Server to Client only, in response to CONNECT (Table 2-1, section 2.1.2). The Server must not send more than one CONNACK in a Network Connection [MQTT-3.2.0-2] (section 3.2, fixed header in 3.2.1).

prompt: What packet type number identifies PUBACK in MQTT 5.0, which QoS level is it used for, and can both clients and brokers send it?

expect.direction: Client to Server or Server to Client

provenance: Type value from section 3.4.1, purpose from section 3.4, direction from Table 2-1 in section 2.1.2.
reference_answer: PUBACK is MQTT Control Packet type 4 (first byte 0x40, flags reserved 0). It is the response to a PUBLISH with QoS 1 (section 3.4, fixed header in 3.4.1). Per Table 2-1 in section 2.1.2 it flows Client to Server or Server to Client, so whichever side receives the QoS 1 PUBLISH sends it.

prompt: Where does PUBREC sit in an MQTT 5.0 QoS 2 handshake, and what is its control packet type value?
provenance: Role from section 3.5 and type value from section 3.5.1 (PUBREC Fixed Header).
reference_answer: PUBREC is MQTT Control Packet type 5 (byte 1 = 0x50, reserved flags 0000). It is the response to a PUBLISH with QoS 2 and is the second packet of the QoS 2 exchange (PUBLISH, PUBREC, PUBREL, PUBCOMP). See sections 3.5 and 3.5.1.

prompt: Which MQTT 5.0 packet closes out a QoS 2 delivery, what type number does it use, and what does it answer?
provenance: Role from section 3.7 and type value from section 3.7.1 (PUBCOMP Fixed Header).
reference_answer: PUBCOMP, MQTT Control Packet type 7 (byte 1 = 0x70), is the response to a PUBREL and is the fourth and final packet of the QoS 2 protocol exchange. See sections 3.7 and 3.7.1.

prompt: In MQTT 5.0, what is the packet type value of SUBACK, who sends it, and how are its result codes laid out relative to the topic filters I subscribed to?
provenance: Type value from section 3.9.1, sender and list of codes from section 3.9, ordering rule from section 3.9.3.
reference_answer: SUBACK is MQTT Control Packet type 9 (byte 1 = 0x90), sent by the Server to the Client (section 3.9, 3.9.1). Its payload carries a list of Reason Codes, one per Topic Filter, in the same order as the Topic Filters in the SUBSCRIBE [MQTT-3.9.3-1] (section 3.9.3).

prompt: What packet type number does UNSUBACK use in MQTT 5.0, and which per-filter code tells me I tried to remove a subscription that wasn't there?
provenance: Type value from section 3.11.1 and the reason code from Table 3-9 in section 3.11.3.
reference_answer: UNSUBACK is MQTT Control Packet type 11 (byte 1 = 0xB0), sent Server to Client (section 3.11; fixed header in 3.11.1). The payload reason code 0x11 (No subscription existed) is returned for a Topic Filter that matched nothing; it is listed in Table 3-9 (section 3.11.3) and, being below 0x80, is a success-range code (section 2.4).

prompt: What exact bytes make up an MQTT 5.0 PINGREQ on the wire, and which side is allowed to send it?
provenance: Byte layout from section 3.12.1 (PINGREQ Fixed Header); the sender from section 3.12.
reference_answer: PINGREQ is two bytes: 0xC0 0x00. Byte 1 holds MQTT Control Packet type 12 with reserved flags 0000, and byte 2 is a Remaining Length of 0, since there is no Variable Header or Payload (section 3.12.1). It is sent from a Client to the Server for Keep Alive (section 3.12).

prompt: Which MQTT 5.0 packet does a broker send back to a keep-alive ping, and what is its type number?
provenance: Purpose and sender from section 3.13; type value and zero Remaining Length from section 3.13.1.
reference_answer: The reply is PINGRESP, MQTT Control Packet type 13. It is sent by the Server to the Client in response to a PINGREQ to show the Server is alive (section 3.13). On the wire it is 0xD0 0x00: reserved flags 0000 and a Remaining Length of 0 (section 3.13.1).

prompt: What is the DISCONNECT packet's type value in MQTT 5.0, can either peer send it, and what should I do if its flag bits aren't zero?

any: client to (?:the )?server or (?:the )?server to (?:the )?client|both directions|either direction

expect.direction: Client to Server or Server to Client

provenance: Type value and the reserved-bit check from section 3.14.1; the sender rule from section 3.14.
reference_answer: DISCONNECT is MQTT Control Packet type 14 (byte 1 = 0xE0). In MQTT 5.0 it can be sent by the Client or the Server as the final packet (section 3.14). Its flag bits are reserved and must be 0; if they are set, respond with a DISCONNECT carrying Reason Code 0x81 (Malformed Packet) [MQTT-3.14.1-1] (section 3.14.1).

prompt: I'm adding enhanced authentication to an MQTT 5.0 client. What is the AUTH packet's type value, which reason codes can it carry, and what must have been in CONNECT for AUTH to be legal?
provenance: Type value from section 3.15.1, reason codes from Table 3-11 in section 3.15.2.1, and the Authentication Method precondition from section 3.15.
reference_answer: AUTH is MQTT Control Packet type 15 (byte 1 = 0xF0, flags 0000; section 3.15.1). Its reason codes are 0x00 Success, 0x18 Continue authentication and 0x19 Re-authenticate (section 3.15.2.1). Sending AUTH is a Protocol Error unless the CONNECT packet contained the same Authentication Method (section 3.15).

prompt: Which bits of the first PUBLISH byte hold DUP, QoS and RETAIN in MQTT 5.0, and what is PUBLISH's type value?
search_query: PUBLISH DUP QoS RETAIN bit positions
provenance: Type value from section 3.3.1; bit positions from sections 3.3.1.1 (DUP), 3.3.1.2 (QoS) and 3.3.1.3 (RETAIN); summary in Table 2-2, section 2.1.3.
reference_answer: PUBLISH is MQTT Control Packet type 3 (high nibble 0011, section 3.3.1). In byte 1 the DUP flag is bit 3 (section 3.3.1.1), QoS occupies bits 2-1 (section 3.3.1.2), and RETAIN is bit 0 (section 3.3.1.3). Table 2-2 in section 2.1.3 summarizes these as the only non-reserved fixed-header flags.

prompt: Which MQTT 5.0 conformance statement forces a client to open every connection with CONNECT, and what label covers a client sending CONNECT twice?
provenance: Both requirements are stated in section 3.1 (CONNECT - Connection Request).
reference_answer: [MQTT-3.1.0-1] in section 3.1 says the first packet a Client sends to the Server after the Network Connection is established must be CONNECT. A Client may send CONNECT only once per connection; the Server must treat a second CONNECT as a Protocol Error and close the connection [MQTT-3.1.0-2], also section 3.1.

prompt: For the MQTT 5.0 message expiry property: what is its identifier, how is the value encoded, what unit is it in, and where can I put it?
provenance: Identifier, type and packet list from Table 2-4 in section 2.2.2.2; units and absent behaviour from section 3.3.2.3.3.
reference_answer: Message Expiry Interval has property identifier 0x02 (2) and is a Four Byte Integer (Table 2-4, section 2.2.2.2). It may appear in PUBLISH and in the Will Properties of CONNECT. The value is the Application Message lifetime in seconds; if the property is absent the message does not expire (section 3.3.2.3.3).

prompt: What does property ID 0x0B mean in MQTT 5.0, how is it encoded, which packets carry it, and what values are legal?
provenance: Name, type and packets from Table 2-4 in section 2.2.2.2; value range and Protocol Error rule from section 3.8.2.1.2.
reference_answer: 0x0B (11) is the Subscription Identifier, encoded as a Variable Byte Integer and carried in PUBLISH and SUBSCRIBE (Table 2-4, section 2.2.2.2). In SUBSCRIBE its value can be 1 to 268,435,455; a value of 0, or including it more than once, is a Protocol Error (section 3.8.2.1.2).

prompt: What's the property identifier and wire type for MQTT 5.0 Receive Maximum, which packets carry it, and what value applies when it's left out?
provenance: Identifier, type and packets from Table 2-4 in section 2.2.2.2; default and zero rule from section 3.1.2.11.3.
reference_answer: Receive Maximum is property 0x21 (33), a Two Byte Integer, used in CONNECT and CONNACK (Table 2-4, section 2.2.2.2). If absent it defaults to 65,535; sending it twice or with value 0 is a Protocol Error (section 3.1.2.11.3). It caps concurrent unacknowledged QoS 1 and QoS 2 publications.

prompt: My MQTT 5.0 client got property 0x13 in CONNACK. What is it, what's its type, and does it change my keep-alive timer?
provenance: Name, type and packet from Table 2-4 in section 2.2.2.2; client obligation from section 3.2.2.3.14.
reference_answer: 0x13 (19) is Server Keep Alive, a Two Byte Integer that appears only in CONNACK (Table 2-4, section 2.2.2.2). If the Server sends it, the Client must use this value instead of the Keep Alive it sent in CONNECT [MQTT-3.2.2-21] (section 3.2.2.3.14).

prompt: When a broker redirects my MQTT 5.0 client with a DISCONNECT, which property holds the other server's address, what is its ID and type, and which reason codes accompany it?
provenance: Identifier, type and redirect reason codes from section 3.14.2.2.5; packet list (CONNACK and DISCONNECT) from Table 2-4 in section 2.2.2.2.
reference_answer: It is Server Reference, property 0x1C (28), a UTF-8 Encoded String (section 3.14.2.2.5). The Server sends it in DISCONNECT with Reason Code 0x9C (Use another server) or 0x9D (Server moved); it may also appear in CONNACK (Table 2-4, section 2.2.2.2). Including it more than once is a Protocol Error.

prompt: What does property identifier 0x15 carry in MQTT 5.0, what type is it, and which packets use it?
provenance: Name, type and packets from Table 2-4 in section 2.2.2.2; the AUTH omission rule from section 3.15.2.2.2.
reference_answer: 0x15 (21) is the Authentication Method, a UTF-8 Encoded String naming the extended authentication method. It is used in CONNECT, CONNACK and AUTH (Table 2-4, section 2.2.2.2). In an AUTH packet, omitting it or including it more than once is a Protocol Error (section 3.15.2.2.2).

prompt: For MQTT 5.0 request/response, what is the identifier and data type of the property I use to match replies to requests, and may the broker modify it?

forbidden.note: The Server must forward Correlation Data unaltered.

provenance: Identifier and type from Table 2-4 in section 2.2.2.2; the forwarding rule from section 3.3.2.3.6.
reference_answer: Use Correlation Data, property 0x09 (9), typed as Binary Data and allowed in PUBLISH and Will Properties (Table 2-4, section 2.2.2.2). The Server must send it unaltered to all subscribers receiving the message [MQTT-3.3.2-16]; only the requester and responder interpret it (section 3.3.2.3.6).

prompt: What is property 0x01 in an MQTT 5.0 PUBLISH, what values can it take, and what reason code reports a payload that doesn't match it?
provenance: Name and type from Table 2-4 in section 2.2.2.2; values and the 0x99 reason code from section 3.3.2.3.2.
reference_answer: 0x01 is the Payload Format Indicator, a single Byte (Table 2-4, section 2.2.2.2). Value 0 means the payload is unspecified bytes; value 1 means it is UTF-8 Encoded Character Data. A receiver that validates and finds a mismatch may reply with Reason Code 0x99 (Payload format invalid) (section 3.3.2.3.2).

prompt: Which MQTT 5.0 property lets a client cap the size of packets the broker sends it, what's its identifier and encoding, and is zero allowed?
provenance: All facts come from section 3.1.2.11.4 (Maximum Packet Size in CONNECT), with the packet list in Table 2-4, section 2.2.2.2.
reference_answer: Use Maximum Packet Size, property 0x27 (39), a Four Byte Integer sent in CONNECT (and also usable in CONNACK per Table 2-4, section 2.2.2.2). Setting it to zero or including it twice is a Protocol Error; if absent, only the protocol's own encoding limits apply (section 3.1.2.11.4).

prompt: In MQTT 5.0 terminology, what exactly is a Will Message and who publishes it?

forbidden.note: The Server, not the Client, publishes the Will Message.

provenance: The definition comes from the Terminology in section 1.2, which points to section 3.1.2.5 for details.
reference_answer: Per section 1.2, a Will Message is an Application Message that is published by the Server after the Network Connection is closed, in cases where the Network Connection is not closed normally. The Client registers it in CONNECT; details are in section 3.1.2.5.

prompt: I received reason code 0x92 from an MQTT 5.0 peer. What does it mean and in which packets can it appear?
provenance: Name, value and packets from Table 2-6 in section 2.4; context from the PUBCOMP Reason Code table in section 3.7.2.1.
reference_answer: 0x92 (146) is Packet Identifier not found (Table 2-6, section 2.4). It is only valid in PUBREL and PUBCOMP, during the QoS 2 release/complete steps. Section 3.7.2.1 notes it is not an error during recovery, but at other times indicates a Session State mismatch between Client and Server.

prompt: My MQTT 5.0 client keeps getting kicked with DISCONNECT reason 0x8E. What does that code mean and who sends it?
provenance: Name and packet from Table 2-6 in section 2.4; meaning and sender from Table 3-10 in section 3.14.2.1.
reference_answer: 0x8E (142) is Session taken over, used only in DISCONNECT (Table 2-6, section 2.4). The Server sends it when another Connection using the same ClientID has connected, causing this Connection to be closed (Table 3-10, section 3.14.2.1). Check for two clients sharing one Client Identifier.

prompt: My MQTT 5.0 publisher got a PUBACK with reason code 0x10. Did the publish fail, and which packets can carry that code?

forbidden.note: Codes below 0x80 indicate success; the message is accepted.

provenance: Meaning and sender from Table 3-4 in section 3.4.2.1; packet list from Table 2-6 in section 2.4.
reference_answer: It did not fail. 0x10 (16) is No matching subscribers: the message is accepted, but there are no subscribers (section 3.4.2.1). It is a success code (below 0x80) valid in PUBACK and PUBREC (Table 2-6, section 2.4), and is sent only by the Server instead of 0x00 Success.

prompt: During MQTT 5.0 enhanced auth, what do AUTH reason codes 0x18 and 0x19 mean, and which side may send 0x19?
provenance: Meanings and senders from Table 3-11 in section 3.15.2.1; packet scope from Table 2-6 in section 2.4.
reference_answer: In AUTH, 0x18 (24) is Continue authentication, sent by Client or Server to continue with another step, and 0x19 (25) is Re-authenticate, sent only by the Client to initiate re-authentication (Table 3-11, section 3.15.2.1). Both are AUTH-only codes (Table 2-6, section 2.4).

prompt: How can an MQTT 5.0 client disconnect cleanly but still have the broker publish its last will? Which DISCONNECT reason code is that?

forbidden.note: 0x00 Normal disconnection suppresses the Will Message.

provenance: Code, name and sender from Table 3-10 in section 3.14.2.1, with the packet list in Table 2-6 of section 2.4.
reference_answer: Send DISCONNECT with Reason Code 0x04 (Disconnect with Will Message). It is sent by the Client when it wants to disconnect but requires the Server to also publish its Will Message (Table 3-10, section 3.14.2.1; Table 2-6, section 2.4).

prompt: A SUBACK from my MQTT 5.0 broker contains 0x9E for one filter. What is that code and where else can it show up?
provenance: Name, value and packets from Table 2-6 in section 2.4; SUBACK meaning from Table 3-8 in section 3.9.3.
reference_answer: 0x9E (158) is Shared Subscriptions not supported. It is valid in SUBACK and DISCONNECT (Table 2-6, section 2.4). In SUBACK it means the Server doesn't support Shared Subscriptions for this Client, so that $share filter was refused (Table 3-8, section 3.9.3).

prompt: What reason code does an MQTT 5.0 broker put in CONNACK when it can't speak the protocol level my client requested?
provenance: Code and packet scope from Table 2-6 in section 2.4; meaning from the Connect Reason Code table in section 3.2.2.2.
reference_answer: It uses Reason Code 0x84 (132), Unsupported Protocol Version, which appears only in CONNACK (Table 2-6, section 2.4). Section 3.2.2.2 says it means the Server does not support the MQTT protocol version requested by the Client. Being 0x80 or above, it is a failure and the connection is closed.

prompt: In MQTT 5.0, what is DISCONNECT reason code 0x00 called, what does it do to a pending will, and can I leave the reason byte out?
provenance: All facts come from Table 3-10 and its surrounding text in section 3.14.2.1.
reference_answer: In DISCONNECT, 0x00 is Normal disconnection: close the connection normally, and the Will Message is not published (section 3.14.2.1). When the code is 0x00 and there are no Properties, the Reason Code and Property Length can be omitted; such a DISCONNECT has a Remaining Length of 0 and the receiver reads it as 0x00 (section 3.14.2.1).

prompt: Which MQTT 5.0 rule says I can't pad a Variable Byte Integer with extra continuation bytes, and how many bytes and what maximum value does that encoding allow?

any: four bytes|4 bytes|maximum number of bytes[^.]{0,50}four

provenance: Requirement label, byte limit and value range all come from section 1.5.5 (Variable Byte Integer) and its Table 1-1.
reference_answer: [MQTT-1.5.5-1] in section 1.5.5 requires the encoded value to use the minimum number of bytes necessary. Each byte carries 7 data bits plus a continuation bit, the field is at most four bytes, and the largest encodable value is 268,435,455 (0xFF 0xFF 0xFF 0x7F), per Table 1-1 in section 1.5.5.

prompt: How does MQTT 5.0 define a Malformed Packet versus a Protocol Error, and which DISCONNECT/CONNACK reason codes correspond to each?
provenance: Definitions come from the Terminology in section 1.2; the reason code values from Table 2-6 in section 2.4.
reference_answer: Per section 1.2, a Malformed Packet is a control packet that cannot be parsed according to the specification, while a Protocol Error is detected after the packet has been parsed, when it holds data the protocol disallows or that conflicts with Client/Server state. Table 2-6 (section 2.4) assigns 0x81 Malformed Packet and 0x82 Protocol Error, both valid in CONNACK and DISCONNECT; handling is in section 4.13.

prompt: My broker's string decoder sometimes sees U+0000 or lone UTF-16 surrogate code points inside client IDs and topics. Are these legal in MQTT 5 strings, and how should the receiver classify such a packet?

any: must not include an encoding of the null character
must not include encodings of code points between u\+d800 and u\+dfff

forbidden.note: U+0000 is an absolute MUST NOT, not a SHOULD NOT.

search_query: null character or surrogate in utf-8 string
provenance: Answer key from section 1.5.4 (UTF-8 Encoded String) of MQTT 5.0.
reference_answer: Neither is legal (section 1.5.4). A UTF-8 Encoded String MUST NOT include an encoding of the null character U+0000 [MQTT-1.5.4-2]. The character data must be well-formed UTF-8 and MUST NOT include encodings of code points between U+D800 and U+DFFF [MQTT-1.5.4-1]. A receiver (Client or Server) that gets either one treats the packet as a Malformed Packet and handles it per section 4.13.

prompt: If an incoming MQTT string begins with the bytes EF BB BF, is my parser allowed to drop that byte-order-mark before handing the value to the application?

any: must not be skipped over or stripped

forbidden.note: The spec forbids skipping or stripping the BOM.

search_query: byte order mark in utf-8 string
provenance: Answer key from section 1.5.4 (UTF-8 Encoded String).
reference_answer: Section 1.5.4 says the sequence 0xEF 0xBB 0xBF is always interpreted as U+FEFF (ZERO WIDTH NO-BREAK SPACE) wherever it appears in a string. A packet receiver MUST NOT be skipping or stripping it either [MQTT-1.5.4-3]; it MUST NOT be stripped off, so pass it through as part of the string value.

prompt: To keep my encoder simple I'd like to always emit Remaining Length as a fixed 4-byte field, padding with continuation bytes (e.g. 0x80 0x80 0x80 0x00 for zero). Is that permitted?

any: must use the minimum number of bytes

forbidden.note: Minimal encoding is a MUST, not a SHOULD.

search_query: variable byte integer padding minimum bytes
provenance: Answer key from section 1.5.5 (Variable Byte Integer).
reference_answer: No. Remaining Length is a Variable Byte Integer (section 2.1.4), and section 1.5.5 states the encoded value MUST use the minimum number of bytes necessary to represent the value [MQTT-1.5.5-1]. Zero is therefore the single byte 0x00, and values up to 127 take one byte. The field is at most four bytes long (maximum 268,435,455).

prompt: For QoS 0 publishes, should my client still include a packet identifier in the variable header so I can track them in logs?

any: must not contain a packet identifier

forbidden.note: Including a Packet Identifier in a QoS 0 PUBLISH is prohibited.

provenance: Answer key from section 2.2.1 (Packet Identifier).
reference_answer: No. Per section 2.2.1, a PUBLISH packet MUST NOT contain a Packet Identifier if its QoS value is 0 [MQTT-2.2.1-2]. The Packet Identifier field is present in PUBLISH only when QoS > 0 (Table 2-3). Track QoS 0 messages with your own application-level metadata instead.

prompt: How should my client choose packet IDs for SUBSCRIBE, UNSUBSCRIBE and QoS 1/2 PUBLISH, and at what point can an ID go back into the free pool?

any: must assign it a non-zero packet identifier that is currently unused
pubcomp or a pubrec with a reason code of 128 or greater

search_query: when can a packet id be reused
provenance: Answer key from section 2.2.1 (Packet Identifier).
reference_answer: Section 2.2.1: each time the Client sends a new SUBSCRIBE, UNSUBSCRIBE or QoS > 0 PUBLISH it MUST assign a non-zero Packet Identifier that is currently unused [MQTT-2.2.1-3]. IDs for PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE and UNSUBSCRIBE share one set per side of the Session. An ID becomes available for reuse after the sender processes the matching acknowledgement: PUBACK for QoS 1; PUBCOMP or a PUBREC with a Reason Code of 128 (0x80) or greater for QoS 2; SUBACK or UNSUBACK for SUBSCRIBE/UNSUBSCRIBE.

prompt: Our broker got a PINGREQ whose lower nibble in the first byte is 0x1 rather than zero. What does MQTT 5 require of those bits, and what should the broker do with the packet?

any: must be set to the value listed

provenance: Answer key from section 2.1.3 (Flags) and section 4.13.1 (Malformed Packet and Protocol Errors).
reference_answer: For PINGREQ the four flag bits are Reserved and listed as 0000 in Table 2-2 (section 2.1.3). Reserved flag bits MUST be set to the value listed [MQTT-2.1.3-1], and receiving invalid flags makes it a Malformed Packet. Per section 4.13.1 the Server MUST close the Network Connection [MQTT-4.13.1-1]; it SHOULD send DISCONNECT with Reason Code 0x81 (Malformed Packet) first.

prompt: A buggy client sends a second CONNECT on a TCP connection that is already established and accepted. What is my broker obliged to do?

any: must process a second connect packet[^.]{0,40}protocol error

provenance: Answer key from section 3.1 (CONNECT - Connection Request).
reference_answer: Section 3.1: the first packet the Client sends on a Network Connection MUST be a CONNECT [MQTT-3.1.0-1], and a Client may send CONNECT only once per connection. The Server MUST process a second CONNECT as a Protocol Error and close the Network Connection [MQTT-3.1.0-2]; see section 4.13 for error handling (e.g. DISCONNECT 0x82 before closing).

prompt: My client sets an Authentication Method property in CONNECT to do a challenge/response login. Can it pipeline SUBSCRIBE and PUBLISH packets right after CONNECT, before the CONNACK comes back?

any: must not send any packets other than auth or disconnect
(?:\bno\b\s*[,-]\s*(?:(?!\b(?:not|never|no|cannot)\b|n't)[^.;]){0,60}?)?(?:must not|mustn.t|cannot|can.t|may not) send[^.]{0,40}(?:other than|except|besides|apart from|but) AUTH
until it has received a connack

forbidden.note: With an Authentication Method set, only AUTH or DISCONNECT may precede CONNACK.

search_query: authentication method client send before connack
provenance: Answer key from section 3.1.2.11.9 (CONNECT Authentication Method).
reference_answer: No. Per section 3.1.2.11.9, if a Client sets an Authentication Method in CONNECT, the Client MUST NOT send any packets other than AUTH or DISCONNECT [MQTT-3.1.2-30]. That restriction holds until it has received a CONNACK. Pipelining SUBSCRIBE/PUBLISH is only possible once enhanced authentication (section 4.12) completes.

prompt: My client reconnected with Clean Start = 0 but has lost its local session store, and CONNACK reports Session Present = 1. What must the client do? And what if it does have local state but sees Session Present = 0?
search_query: session present flag unexpected value client
provenance: Answer key from section 3.2.2.1.1 (Session Present).
reference_answer: Section 3.2.2.1.1: if the Client has no Session State and receives Session Present = 1, it MUST close the Network Connection [MQTT-3.2.2-4]; to start fresh it can reconnect with Clean Start set to 1. If the Client has Session State and receives Session Present = 0, it MUST discard its Session State if it continues with the Network Connection [MQTT-3.2.2-5].

prompt: The broker's CONNACK carried Maximum QoS = 1, but my application asks to publish at QoS 2. What must the client library do, and what happens if a QoS 2 PUBLISH is sent anyway?

If 90 s pass before onward delivery starts, the interval has passed and the server MUST delete the copy for that subscriber (3.3.2.3.3). Once the PUBLISH has been sent, the sender must not apply message expiry, and the receiver continues the QoS 2 acknowledgement sequence regardless (4.3.3).

prompt: Our client library receives a PUBLISH whose topic name is empty and whose Topic Alias is 3, but nothing was ever mapped to alias 3 on this connection (we just reconnected). How must the client handle it?
search_query: publish with alias and empty topic but no mapping
provenance: Answer key from 3.3.4 (receiver processing of Topic Alias) and 3.3.2.3.4 (alias mappings are per Network Connection).
reference_answer: An unknown alias with a zero-length Topic Name is a Protocol Error (3.3.4): the client sends DISCONNECT with Reason Code 0x82 (Protocol Error) and closes the connection. Mappings from the previous connection are gone, because a receiver must not carry forward alias mappings between network connections (3.3.2.3.4). The sender must first re-establish the alias with a non-empty topic name.

prompt: In CONNECT our client advertised Topic Alias Maximum 5. The broker then sends a PUBLISH using alias 9. What is the correct reaction, and what if we had left the property out entirely?
search_query: broker sent alias bigger than the max i allowed
provenance: Answer key from 3.3.4 (Topic Alias receive processing) and 3.1.2.11.5 (Topic Alias Maximum in CONNECT).
reference_answer: Alias 9 exceeds the maximum you sent, so it is a Protocol Error: disconnect with Reason Code 0x94 (Topic Alias invalid) (3.3.4). The broker must not send a topic alias greater than the Topic Alias Maximum from CONNECT (3.1.2.11.5). Had you omitted the property, the default value is 0, meaning the broker must send no aliases at all (3.1.2.11.5).

prompt: I'm building a bridge that subscribes to '#' on broker A and republishes into broker B, and B back into A, using the same client connection each way. Messages loop back and retained state arrives with RETAIN cleared. Which subscription options fix this?

any: (?:(?<![\s\S])|(?<=[.;:!?]\s)|(?<=\n))[^.;:!?\n]{0,150}?(?:(?:own|same|publishing(?: connection(?:'|’)?s)?) client ?id|client ?id equal to|client ?id is the same)

provenance: Answer key from 3.8.3.1 (No Local and Retain As Published options) and 3.3.1.3 (RETAIN flag when forwarding).
reference_answer: Set No Local (bit 2) to 1 on the bridge's subscriptions. It stops the server forwarding messages to a connection with the same ClientID as the publisher, which breaks the loop (3.8.3.1). Also set Retain As Published (bit 3) to 1: the server then sets the RETAIN flag equal to the RETAIN flag in the received PUBLISH, instead of forcing 0 (3.3.1.3).

prompt: On every reconnect (Clean Start 0) our client blindly re-sends its SUBSCRIBE list in case the earlier one didn't complete, and users complain that retained messages are replayed each time. Which option avoids the replay while still getting retained messages for genuinely new subscriptions?
search_query: avoid getting retained messages again on resubscribe
provenance: Answer key from 3.3.1.3 (Retain Handling behaviour) and 3.8.4 (replacing an identical subscription).
reference_answer: Use Retain Handling = 1 (3.3.1.3, 3.8.3.1). A SUBSCRIBE with an identical filter simply replaces the existing subscription (3.8.4), and with the default Retain Handling 0 any matching retained messages are re-sent each time (3.8.4). With value 1 the server sends retained messages only when the subscription is new. If it already exists the server must not send the retained messages (3.3.1.3).

prompt: A decommissioned device left a retained status message on 'site/7/status'. How do we delete it from the broker, and would publishing a normal non-retained message to that topic have done the trick?
provenance: Answer key from 3.3.1.3 (RETAIN flag handling).
reference_answer: Publish to site/7/status with the RETAIN flag set to 1 and a zero-byte payload. The broker processes it normally but removes the existing retained message, and the empty message itself is never stored as retained, so future subscribers get nothing (3.3.1.3). A PUBLISH with RETAIN 0 would not help: the server must not remove or replace any existing retained message in that case (3.3.1.3).

prompt: Our client holds subscriptions 'a/b' and 'a/+'. It sends one UNSUBSCRIBE listing 'a/#' and 'a/+'. What does the broker remove, what does the reply look like, and are QoS 1 messages already being sent for those filters abandoned?
search_query: unsubscribe filter that was never subscribed
provenance: Answer key from 3.10.4 (UNSUBSCRIBE actions) and 3.11.3 (UNSUBACK payload Reason Codes).
reference_answer: Filters are compared character-by-character, so 'a/+' is deleted while 'a/#' matches nothing and 'a/b' stays (3.10.4). The broker answers with a single UNSUBACK (same Packet Identifier) holding one reason code per filter in request order (3.11.3): 0x11 (No subscription existed) for 'a/#' and 0x00 for 'a/+'. It stops queuing new matches but MUST complete delivery of QoS 1/2 messages already started (3.10.4).

prompt: Our constrained client sets Maximum Packet Size to 1024 in CONNECT. Someone publishes a 4 KB message to a topic we subscribe to at QoS 1. What does the broker do with it, and what should our client do if a too-large packet slips through anyway?

any: as if it had completed sending

search_query: message bigger than client max packet size
provenance: Answer key from 3.1.2.11.4 (CONNECT Maximum Packet Size).
reference_answer: The broker must not send packets exceeding the client's Maximum Packet Size (3.1.2.11.4). It discards the 4 KB message and behaves as if it had completed sending that Application Message, so it is simply dropped for this client (3.1.2.11.4). If the client ever receives a packet over 1024 bytes, that is a Protocol Error: it sends DISCONNECT with Reason Code 0x95 (Packet too large) (3.1.2.11.4).

prompt: During a migration our broker rejects CONNECT with reason 0x9D and includes a Server Reference of 'mq1.example.net:8883 mq2.example.net:8883'. How should the client interpret this compared with 0x9C, and how should it parse that string?
search_query: connack server moved where to reconnect
provenance: Answer key from 4.11 (Server redirection).
reference_answer: 0x9D (Server moved) means the client SHOULD permanently switch to another server, whereas 0x9C (Use another server) asks for a temporary switch (4.11). The Server Reference (3.2.2.3.16) is a space-separated list of references, typically host:port. The client is expected to choose one of them, e.g. mq1 or mq2 on 8883, and update its stored endpoint (4.11). It is also allowed to ignore the reference.

prompt: We're adding a SCRAM-style login: the client's CONNECT includes Authentication Method and initial Authentication Data, and the broker replies with an AUTH packet instead of CONNACK. What should the client send next, what must every AUTH carry, and what may the client send before CONNACK arrives?
search_query: challenge response login with auth packets
provenance: Answer key from 4.12 (Enhanced authentication) and 3.1.2.11.9 (Authentication Method restricts pre-CONNACK packets).
reference_answer: Reply with an AUTH packet using Reason Code 0x18 (Continue authentication) carrying the next Authentication Data (4.12, 3.15.2.1). Every AUTH, and the final successful CONNACK, must include the Authentication Method with the same value as in CONNECT (4.12). Until CONNACK arrives the client may only send AUTH or DISCONNECT packets (3.1.2.11.9). The exchange repeats until the server accepts with a CONNACK with Reason Code 0, or rejects and closes the connection (4.12).

prompt: We're implementing RPC over MQTT: a service listens on 'svc/thermostat/req', and callers expect a reply. How should the caller tag the request so it gets the right answer back, and what must the responder (and the broker in between) do with those properties?
provenance: Answer key from 4.10.1 (Basic Request Response), 3.3.2.3.5 (Response Topic) and 3.3.2.3.6 (Correlation Data).
reference_answer: The caller subscribes to a reply topic, then publishes the request with a Response Topic property naming it (which must not contain wildcard characters) and a Correlation Data value identifying the call (3.3.2.3.5, 3.3.2.3.6, 4.10.1). The broker forwards both properties unaltered to every subscriber (3.3.2.3.6). The responder publishes its answer to the Response Topic and copies the Correlation Data into the response so the caller can match it (4.10.1).

prompt: Walk me through a QoS 2 exchange from both the sender's and receiver's side: which packets flow, when is the packet ID free again, and what has to be resent if the client reconnects and the session is still there?
provenance: Answer key from sections 4.3.3 (QoS 2 sender/receiver rules) and 4.4 (message delivery retry).
reference_answer: The sender stores the message and sends PUBLISH QoS 2 with DUP=0 and an unused Packet Identifier. The receiver answers with PUBREC; the sender then sends PUBREL with the same identifier and must never re-send the PUBLISH after that. The receiver answers PUBREL with PUBCOMP, and must not deliver duplicates onward while waiting for PUBREL (4.3.3). The identifier becomes available for reuse after the PUBCOMP arrives (or after a PUBREC with Reason Code 0x80 or above). If the client reconnects with Clean Start 0 and a session is present, both sides resend unacknowledged PUBLISH and PUBREL packets using their original Packet Identifiers (4.4).

prompt: My client's last-will is configured with a 60 second delay, but its session expiry is only 30 seconds. If the network drops, when does the will actually go out, does reconnecting quickly stop it, and what changes if the client disconnects cleanly?
search_query: last will timing when session expires first
provenance: Answer key from sections 3.1.3.2.2 (will delay behaviour) and 3.1.2.5 (Will Flag, deletion on normal disconnect).
reference_answer: The Server holds the Will Message until the Will Delay Interval passes or the Session ends, whichever happens first (3.1.3.2.2). With a 60 s delay and 30 s Session Expiry, the will is therefore published at about 30 s, when the Session ends. If the client reconnects to that Session before then, the Server must not send the Will Message. A DISCONNECT with Reason Code 0x00 (Normal disconnection) makes the Server discard the stored will entirely (3.1.2.5); a client that still wants it published can disconnect with 0x04 instead.

prompt: How does Receive Maximum throttle a publisher in MQTT 5? I want to know how the in-flight budget goes down and back up, what the default is, whether QoS 0 traffic is limited, and what the peer does if I overrun it.
provenance: Answer key from sections 4.9 (flow control and send quota), 3.3.4 (PUBLISH actions, 0x93) and 3.1.2.11.3 (Receive Maximum default).
reference_answer: Each side advertises Receive Maximum in CONNECT or CONNACK; when absent it defaults to 65,535 (3.1.2.11.3). The sender starts with a send quota up to that value and decrements the send quota for every QoS 1 or QoS 2 PUBLISH; at zero it must stop sending QoS>0 PUBLISH packets but keep processing other packets (4.9). The quota goes up by one for each PUBACK or PUBCOMP received, even with an error code, and for each PUBREC carrying 0x80 or above. QoS 0 is exempt: a sender may continue to send QoS 0 messages at zero quota, or choose to pause them. The quota and Receive Maximum are not preserved across Network Connections. A receiver that gets more than Receive Maximum unacknowledged QoS>0 PUBLISH packets disconnects with Reason Code 0x93 (Receive Maximum exceeded, 3.3.4).

prompt: We run three worker clients in one $share group. How does the broker decide who gets each message, do newly joined workers get retained messages, and what happens if a worker rejects a message with an error ack or loses its connection halfway through a QoS 2 delivery?
provenance: Answer key from sections 4.8.2 (shared subscription delivery and acknowledgement rules) and 3.8.4 (SUBSCRIBE actions for shared filters).
reference_answer: A message matching $share/{ShareName}/{filter} goes to one and only one Session in the group, and the Server is free to choose which, message by message (4.8.2). No retained messages are sent when a Session joins a shared subscription (3.8.4). If a worker returns PUBACK or PUBREC with a Reason Code of 0x80 or greater, the Server must discard the message and not try another member. If a QoS 2 delivery is interrupted, the Server must complete the delivery to that same client when it reconnects; if that Session ends first, the message is not sent to anyone else (4.8.2).

prompt: How do I build an RPC-style call over MQTT 5? Which properties should the requester set, what should the responder copy back, and can the broker help a client choose its reply topic?
search_query: request reply correlation id reply topic
provenance: Answer key from sections 4.10 and 4.10.1 (request/response pattern), 3.3.2.3.5 (Response Topic), 3.3.2.3.6 (Correlation Data), 3.1.2.11.6 (Request Response Information) and 3.2.2.3.15 (Response Information).
reference_answer: The requester publishes the request with a Response Topic property (a topic name; it must not contain wildcards, 3.3.2.3.5) and usually Correlation Data, binary data identifying the request (3.3.2.3.6). The Server forwards both unaltered. The responder publishes its reply to that Response Topic and should copy the Correlation Data unaltered into the response so the requester can match it (4.10.1). To get help choosing a reply topic, the client sets Request Response Information to 1 in CONNECT (3.1.2.11.6); the Server may then put Response Information in the CONNACK, but this is optional (3.2.2.3.15) and how the client turns it into a topic is up to the application.

prompt: What does the MQTT 5 spec recommend for locking down a broker deployment: which port for TLS, the ways clients can prove who they are, how a client can trust the broker, and what authorization checks the broker should make?
provenance: Answer key from sections 5.1 (security introduction, port 8883), 5.4.1 (client authentication), 5.4.2 (authorization), 5.4.3 (server authentication) and 5.4.5 (privacy).
reference_answer: Chapter 5 is non-normative guidance. Servers offering TLS should use TCP port 8883 (5.1). Clients can be authenticated with the CONNECT User Name and Password fields (checked against LDAP, OAuth tokens or the OS), with TLS client certificates, or with enhanced authentication (5.4.1). After authentication the Server should check authorization, notably that the client may use its Client Identifier, and restrict publishing and subscribing to particular topics, especially broad # filters (5.4.2). Basic authentication gives the client no way to verify the Server; use TLS server certificates, plus the Server Name Indication extension when several hostnames share one IP (5.4.3). For privacy, avoid TLS cipher suites with NULL encryption (5.4.5).

prompt: How does a SCRAM-style challenge/response login work in MQTT 5, and can my client refresh its credentials later on without tearing down the connection?

any: (?:\bno\b\s*[,-]\s*(?:(?!\b(?:not|never|no|cannot)\b|n't)[^.;]){0,60}?)?(?:must not|mustn't|may not|cannot|can't) send (?:any(?:thing|\s+packets)?\s+)?(?:packets\s+)?(?:other than|except|besides|but) AUTH (?:or|and) DISCONNECT

provenance: Answer key from sections 4.12 (enhanced authentication), 4.12.1 (re-authentication) and 3.1.2.11.9 (Authentication Method in CONNECT).
reference_answer: Enhanced authentication starts when the client puts an Authentication Method (for example SCRAM-SHA-1) and optionally Authentication Data in CONNECT (4.12). Until CONNACK arrives the client must not send anything other than AUTH or DISCONNECT packets (3.1.2.11.9). The Server may answer with AUTH carrying Reason Code 0x18 (Continue authentication) and challenge data; the client replies with AUTH 0x18, and this repeats until the Server accepts by sending a CONNACK with Reason Code 0 (Success). Every AUTH and the successful CONNACK must carry the same Authentication Method as CONNECT. Later the client can re-authenticate at any time by sending AUTH with Reason Code 0x19 using the same method; the Server replies with 0x18 or 0x00, and other traffic continues using the previous authentication meanwhile (4.12.1). A failed re-authentication closes the connection.

prompt: We're carrying MQTT from browsers over WebSockets. What framing and subprotocol rules must both ends follow, and is that part of the spec mandatory for a library that claims to be a conformant client?
provenance: Answer key from section 6 (WebSocket transport rules) and section 7.1.2 (Client conformance clause).
reference_answer: Under Chapter 6, MQTT packets must travel in WebSocket binary data frames; if any other frame type arrives the recipient must close the Network Connection. One frame may hold several or partial MQTT packets, so receivers must not assume packets are aligned with frame boundaries. The client must offer “mqtt” as a WebSocket subprotocol, and the Server must select and return mqtt. The WebSocket URI has no effect on MQTT itself; IANA registers the identifier as mqtt (6.1). Chapter 6 is mandatory for conformance: the client clause (7.1.2) requires all MUST-level requirements of Chapters 1-4 and Chapter 6 that apply to clients, and the server clause (7.1.1) lists it too.

prompt: What exactly must a broker satisfy to call itself a conformant MQTT 5 server, how is that different from what a client library must satisfy, and does either one have to implement the security chapter?
provenance: Answer key from sections 7 (conformance overview), 7.1.1 (Server clause), 7.1.2 (Client clause) and 5.1 (security chapter is non-normative).
reference_answer: Chapter 7 defines separate clauses, and one implementation can conform as both a Client and a Server. A conformant Server (7.1.1) must send packets whose format matches Chapter 2 and Chapter 3, follow the topic matching rules of 4.7 and the subscription rules of 4.8, meet every MUST-level requirement in Chapters 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 except those that only apply to the Client, and must not require any extensions defined outside the specification to interoperate. The Client clause (7.1.2) is the same minus the topic-matching and subscription item, excluding requirements that only apply to the Server. Neither clause lists the security chapter: Chapter 5 is non-normative guidance (5.1).

prompt: I'm writing a parser for MQTT 5 properties. How are variable-length integers, text strings, binary blobs and user-property pairs laid out on the wire, and what are the size limits of each?
search_query: variable byte integer encoding string length prefix
provenance: Answer key from sections 1.5.2 (Two Byte Integer), 1.5.4 (UTF-8 Encoded String), 1.5.5 (Variable Byte Integer), 1.5.6 (Binary Data) and 1.5.7 (UTF-8 String Pair).
reference_answer: Variable Byte Integers carry 7 data bits per byte, with the most significant bit used as a continuation bit; the maximum is four bytes, covering 0 to 268,435,455, and encoders must use the minimum number of bytes (1.5.5). Two and Four Byte Integers are big-endian (1.5.2, 1.5.3). A UTF-8 Encoded String is prefixed by a Two Byte Integer length, so it holds 0 to 65,535 bytes (1.5.4); Binary Data uses the same two-byte length prefix and limit (1.5.6). A UTF-8 String Pair, used by User Property, is two such strings forming a name-value pair, and both must be valid UTF-8 strings or the packet is malformed (1.5.7).

prompt: My client requests a 120 second keep alive, but the broker's CONNACK comes back with a different keep-alive value. Which one wins, how do pings fit in, and at what point will the broker cut me off?
provenance: Answer key from sections 3.1.2.10 (Keep Alive), 3.2.2.3.14 (Server Keep Alive), 3.12.4 (PINGREQ actions) and 3.14.2.1 (Disconnect Reason Codes).
reference_answer: Keep Alive in CONNECT is the longest gap allowed between client packets; if nothing else is due the client must send PINGREQ, and the Server must answer each PINGREQ with PINGRESP (3.12.4). If the CONNACK contains Server Keep Alive, the client must use that value instead of its own 120 s (3.2.2.3.14); otherwise the Server uses the client's value. If the Server receives nothing within one and a half times the effective Keep Alive, it must close the connection as if the network had failed (3.1.2.10), and it can signal this with DISCONNECT 0x8D (Keep Alive timeout, 3.14.2.1).

prompt: A client holds several overlapping wildcard subscriptions, each with its own QoS and subscription identifier. When one publication matches all of them, what QoS does it arrive at and which identifiers come along with it?
provenance: Answer key from sections 3.3.4 (PUBLISH actions for overlapping subscriptions), 3.8.4 (SUBSCRIBE actions, QoS downgrade) and 3.3.2.3.8 (Subscription Identifier range).
reference_answer: When overlapping subscriptions match, the Server must deliver the message respecting the maximum QoS of all the matching subscriptions, and may in addition send further copies, one per matching subscription at that subscription's QoS (3.3.4). Each delivery's QoS is the minimum of the published QoS and the granted maximum (3.8.4). If one copy is sent it carries the Subscription Identifiers for all matching subscriptions that have one, and their order is not significant; with multiple copies each carries its own subscription's identifier. Identifiers range from 1 to 268,435,455 (3.3.2.3.8), and a PUBLISH sent by a client to the Server must not contain a Subscription Identifier.

prompt: During a data-centre migration our broker needs to move clients to a new host. How does it tell clients whether the move is temporary or permanent, and how does it say where to reconnect?
provenance: Answer key from sections 4.11 (server redirection) and 3.14.2.2.5 (Server Reference property).
reference_answer: The Server can redirect with a CONNACK or DISCONNECT carrying Reason Code 0x9C (Use another server), meaning switch temporarily, or 0x9D (Server moved), meaning switch permanently (4.11). It may add a Server Reference property (3.14.2.2.5), a UTF-8 string holding a space-separated list of references such as host:port, from which the client should pick one. Sending a Server Reference is optional, and the client is allowed to ignore it.

prompt: My client tells the broker it can only take 1 KB packets, yet a 5 KB message matches one of its subscriptions. What does the broker do with it, and what happens in the opposite direction if my client sends something larger than the broker's limit?
provenance: Answer key from sections 3.1.2.11.4 (client Maximum Packet Size), 3.2.2.3.6 (server Maximum Packet Size) and 2.1.4 (packet size definition).
reference_answer: Maximum Packet Size counts the whole packet, meaning the total number of bytes: fixed header plus Remaining Length (2.1.4). Since the client advertised 1 KB in CONNECT, the Server must discard the 5 KB message, sending nothing, and then behave as if it had completed sending it (3.1.2.11.4); for a shared subscription it may instead give it to another member able to receive it. Conversely, the client must respect the Server's CONNACK limit; a Server receiving an oversize packet treats it as a Protocol Error and uses DISCONNECT with Reason Code 0x95 (Packet too large) (3.2.2.3.6).

prompt: When my client reconnects with clean start off and a non-zero session expiry, how can it tell whether the broker kept its old session, and what should it do if the broker's answer disagrees with what the client itself has stored?
provenance: Answer key from sections 3.2.2.1.1 (Session Present), 3.1.2.4 (Clean Start) and 3.1.2.11.2 (Session Expiry Interval storage rule).
reference_answer: With Clean Start 0 the Server resumes an existing Session or creates a new one (3.1.2.4). State survives a disconnection only when Session Expiry Interval is greater than 0, since both sides must store the Session State after the connection closes in that case (3.1.2.11.2). The CONNACK Session Present flag tells you: the Server sets Session Present to 1 if it had state for the ClientID, otherwise 0; with Clean Start 1 it is always set to 0. A client lacking state that sees 1 must close the Network Connection; a client holding state that sees 0 must discard its Session State if it continues (3.2.2.1.1).

prompt: Is it legal for a client to connect with an empty client ID? If the broker goes along with it, how does the client find out what identifier it ended up with?

forbidden.note: Accepting a zero-length ClientID is optional for the Server, not forbidden.

provenance: Answer key from sections 3.1.3.1 (Client Identifier) and 3.2.2.3.7 (Assigned Client Identifier).
reference_answer: Yes, optionally. A Server may allow a zero-length ClientID; if it does, it must treat it as a special case, assign a unique ClientID and process the CONNECT as if the client had supplied it (3.1.3.1), returning it in the CONNACK's Assigned Client Identifier property, which must be new to every other Session on the Server (3.2.2.3.7). A Server that refuses it may send CONNACK with Reason Code 0x85 (Client Identifier not valid) and must close the Network Connection. Servers are only obliged to accept 1-23 alphanumeric characters.

prompt: My receiver just got a PUBLISH whose alias value is 0, another whose alias exceeds the maximum I advertised, and a third with an alias I've never seen plus an empty topic name. How should I treat each?

forbidden.note: An invalid alias is a Protocol Error leading to DISCONNECT, not something to skip.

provenance: Answer key from sections 3.3.4 (receiver processing of Topic Alias) and 3.3.2.3.4 (Topic Alias property).
reference_answer: All three are errors. A Topic Alias of 0 is not permitted, and an alias greater than the Topic Alias Maximum the receiver advertised is likewise invalid: both are a Protocol Error and the receiver uses DISCONNECT with Reason Code 0x94 (Topic Alias invalid) (3.3.4, 3.3.2.3.4). An unmapped alias arriving with a zero-length Topic Name is also a Protocol Error, answered with DISCONNECT 0x82. Mappings exist only within a single Network Connection, so an alias set on an earlier connection is unknown after reconnecting.

prompt: Why does my '#' subscription never see the broker's $SYS statistics, and what would I have to subscribe to in order to get those as well as my normal topics?

forbidden.note: Wildcard-leading filters never match $ topics.

provenance: Answer key from section 4.7.2 (Topics beginning with $).
reference_answer: Topic Filters starting with a wildcard (# or +) must not match Topic Names beginning with $, so '#' never receives $SYS/... messages (4.7.2), even though '#' otherwise matches every topic (4.7.1.2). Subscribe to $SYS/# (or a narrower filter such as $SYS/monitor/+) to get them; to receive both kinds, subscribe to both # and $SYS/#. Applications cannot use a topic with a leading $ for their own purposes, since servers reserve such names.

prompt: Can a PUBLISH ever carry an empty topic name, and is an empty topic filter acceptable in a SUBSCRIBE?

forbidden.note: Topic Filters must be at least one character long.

provenance: Answer key from sections 4.7.3 (topic length rule), 3.3.2.1 (Topic Name) and 3.3.4 (alias processing).
reference_answer: Never for filters, and only with an alias for names. Every Topic Name and Topic Filter must be at least one character long (4.7.3), so an empty filter in SUBSCRIBE is invalid. In PUBLISH, a zero-length Topic Name is allowed solely when a Topic Alias is present and already mapped; a zero-length name lacking any alias is a Protocol Error (3.3.2.1), and an unmapped alias with an empty name is a Protocol Error answered with DISCONNECT 0x82 (3.3.4).

prompt: One client puts U+0000 in a topic, another sends a lone UTF-16 surrogate encoded in a string, and a third uses the bell character U+0007. Which of these must a receiver reject, and which is optional?

any: (?:not required|not obliged|not mandatory|not mandated) to validate

forbidden.note: Control characters are SHOULD NOT; receivers MAY treat them as malformed.

search_query: null character surrogate control characters strings
provenance: Answer key from sections 1.5.4 (UTF-8 Encoded String rules) and 5.4.9 (handling of Disallowed Unicode code points).
reference_answer: U+0000 is never allowed in a UTF-8 Encoded String, and encodings of the surrogate range U+D800 to U+DFFF make the string ill-formed; a receiver treats either as a Malformed Packet (1.5.4). U+0007 is different: control characters U+0001-U+001F are Disallowed Unicode code points that senders should avoid, and a receiver may treat them as malformed but is free to accept them. Implementations can choose whether to validate these code points (5.4.9); if the broker skips validation but a subscriber validates, a publisher can make that subscriber drop its connection.

prompt: What is the biggest packet MQTT 5 can encode, and is it valid for the remaining-length field to use a fifth byte or to be padded with more bytes than it needs?

forbidden.note: Remaining Length tops out at 268,435,455, not 2^32-1.

provenance: Answer key from sections 1.5.5 (Variable Byte Integer) and 2.1.4 (Remaining Length).
reference_answer: The Remaining Length is a Variable Byte Integer of at most four bytes, so its maximum is 268,435,455 (0xFF 0xFF 0xFF 0x7F) (1.5.5). It does not include the bytes used to encode itself, so the whole packet is that plus the fixed header (2.1.4), roughly 256 MB. A fifth continuation byte makes the Variable Byte Integer malformed, and encoders must use the minimum number of bytes, so a padded encoding is also non-compliant.

prompt: Can my client and the broker both have packet identifier 0x1234 in flight simultaneously? And may I reuse an identifier that an earlier unacknowledged SUBSCRIBE is still using?

forbidden.note: Client and Server identifier spaces are independent.

provenance: Answer key from sections 2.2.1 (Packet Identifier) and 3.4.2.1 (PUBACK Reason Codes, 0x91).
reference_answer: Yes to the first: Client and Server assign Packet Identifiers independently, so both may have 0x1234 in flight at once (2.2.1). Within one side, though, PUBLISH (QoS>0), SUBSCRIBE and UNSUBSCRIBE draw from one unified set of identifiers, and an identifier cannot be used by more than one command at a time; it becomes reusable only after the matching acknowledgement, which for SUBSCRIBE is the SUBACK. New identifiers must be non-zero. A receiver that detects a clash can reply with Reason Code 0x91 (Packet identifier in use) (3.4.2.1).

prompt: Should a subscriber send a PUBACK back for a QoS 0 message it receives, and does a QoS 0 PUBLISH even have a packet identifier?

forbidden.note: QoS 0 has no acknowledgement.

provenance: Answer key from sections 3.3.4 (expected PUBLISH response), 2.2.1 (Packet Identifier presence) and 4.3.1 (QoS 0 delivery).
reference_answer: No. QoS 0 means at most once delivery. The expected response to a QoS 0 PUBLISH is None, so the receiver sends nothing back and the sender performs no retry (3.3.4, 4.3.1). PUBACK belongs to QoS 1 and PUBREC to QoS 2. A QoS 0 PUBLISH must not contain a Packet Identifier (2.2.1) and must be sent with the DUP flag set to 0 (4.3.1).

prompt: What does a session expiry of 0xFFFFFFFF mean, and what happens if I connected with expiry 0 but then put a non-zero session expiry into my DISCONNECT? Can the broker send me a session expiry in its own DISCONNECT?

forbidden.note: 0xFFFFFFFF means the session never expires.

search_query: session never expires disconnect change expiry
provenance: Answer key from sections 3.1.2.11.2 (Session Expiry Interval in CONNECT) and 3.14.2.2.2 (Session Expiry Interval in DISCONNECT).
reference_answer: Session Expiry 0xFFFFFFFF (UINT_MAX) means the Session does not expire (3.1.2.11.2). If CONNECT carried a Session Expiry Interval of 0 (or omitted it), the client is barred from setting a non-zero value in DISCONNECT: that is a Protocol Error, and the Server rejects it and uses DISCONNECT with Reason Code 0x82 (3.14.2.2.2). The Server must not send a Session Expiry Interval in its own DISCONNECT. A non-zero CONNECT value can be changed at DISCONNECT.

prompt: If my client sets keep alive to zero, will the broker ever drop it for being idle, and do I still need to send pings?

forbidden.note: Keep Alive settings do not guarantee the client stays connected.

provenance: Answer key from sections 3.1.2.10 (Keep Alive) and 3.2.2.3.14 (Server Keep Alive).
reference_answer: Keep Alive 0 turns off the keep-alive mechanism: the 1.5x inactivity timeout is off and the client is not obliged to send packets on any schedule, so PINGREQ is optional (3.1.2.10). However, if the CONNACK includes a Server Keep Alive the client must use that value instead (3.2.2.3.14). Keep Alive is also no promise of staying connected; the Server may have other reasons to disconnect you, such as shutting down.

prompt: Can I send subscription identifier 0 to mean 'no identifier'? What values are allowed, and what happens if the broker doesn't support identifiers at all?

forbidden.note: Value 0 is a Protocol Error.

provenance: Answer key from sections 3.8.2.1.2 (Subscription Identifier in SUBSCRIBE) and 3.2.2.3.12 (Subscription Identifiers Available).
reference_answer: No. A Subscription Identifier of 0 is a Protocol Error; valid values are 1 to 268,435,455 (3.8.2.1.2). To have no identifier, leave the property out: the absence of an identifier is then stored with the subscription. Check Subscription Identifiers Available in CONNACK (3.2.2.3.12); if the Server lacks support, a SUBSCRIBE carrying one is a Protocol Error and the Server uses DISCONNECT with Reason Code 0xA1 (Subscription Identifiers not supported).

prompt: A publisher marks its payload as UTF-8 text via the format indicator but actually sends raw binary. What are the broker and the subscribers allowed to do, and should the broker correct the flag before forwarding?

forbidden.note: The Server must send the indicator unaltered.

provenance: Answer key from sections 3.3.2.3.2 (Payload Format Indicator) and 5.4.9 (validation asymmetry security note).
reference_answer: The broker must forward the Payload Format Indicator unaltered to all subscribers (3.3.2.3.2). Any receiver (the Server, or a subscribing client) may validate that the payload matches the indicator and on a mismatch respond with PUBACK, PUBREC, or DISCONNECT using Reason Code 0x99 (Payload format invalid). Beware the asymmetry in 5.4.9: if a subscriber validates the payload but the Server does not, a bad publisher can make that subscriber close its connection.

prompt: What should a broker do if a client sends CONNECT again on a connection that's already up? Is that handled like a second connection arriving with the same client ID?

forbidden.note: A second CONNECT is a Protocol Error, not a way to update the session.

provenance: Answer key from sections 3.1 (CONNECT once per connection), 3.1.4 (CONNECT actions, takeover) and 4.13.1 (protocol error handling).
reference_answer: A client may send CONNECT only once per Network Connection; the Server must treat a second CONNECT as a Protocol Error and close the Network Connection (3.1), optionally sending DISCONNECT with Reason Code 0x82 first (4.13.1). Re-authentication uses AUTH with 0x19 instead. That differs from a new connection using the same ClientID: there the Server sends the existing client DISCONNECT 0x8E (Session taken over) and closes the old connection (3.1.4).

prompt: Is the broker allowed to send DISCONNECT before it has sent CONNACK? Once connected, which reason codes might it use when kicking me off, and may it include a session expiry value?

forbidden.note: 0x04 is sent only by the Client.

provenance: Answer key from sections 3.14 (DISCONNECT overview), 3.14.2.1 (Disconnect Reason Codes) and 3.14.2.2.2 (Session Expiry Interval in DISCONNECT).
reference_answer: The Server must not send a DISCONNECT until after its CONNACK. That CONNACK must have a Reason Code less than 0x80 (3.14); before then, rejections go in the CONNACK itself. Afterwards it may disconnect with codes such as 0x8B (Server shutting down), 0x8D (Keep Alive timeout), 0x8E (Session taken over), 0x9C/0x9D for redirection, or 0x81/0x82 for errors (3.14.2.1). 0x04 (Disconnect with Will Message) is Client-only. The Server must never send a Session Expiry Interval property on its DISCONNECT (3.14.2.2.2).

prompt: My broker receives a SUBSCRIBE carrying a Topic Alias property, or a property ID it doesn't recognize at all. How should it react? And what if a CONNECT includes Receive Maximum twice?

forbidden.note: An identifier not valid for the packet is a Malformed Packet.

search_query: property not allowed for packet type
provenance: Answer key from sections 2.2.2.2 (Property validity), 4.13.1 (Malformed Packet and Protocol Error handling) and 3.1.2.11.3 (Receive Maximum duplication).
reference_answer: Including a property whose identifier is invalid for the packet type (such as a Topic Alias in SUBSCRIBE, or an unrecognised identifier) makes it a Malformed Packet (2.2.2.2). The receiver responds with CONNACK or DISCONNECT carrying Reason Code 0x81 (Malformed Packet); a Server must close the Network Connection (4.13.1). Including a single-instance property such as Receive Maximum more than once is a Protocol Error (3.1.2.11.3), handled the same way but with Reason Code 0x82.
